extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners (and practitioners referencing MPEP guidance)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for examining claimed inventions for patentability under 35 U.S.C. §§ 101, 102, 103, 112 and related statutes, including claim construction and subject-matter eligibility analyses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Best mode disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: If the inventor did possess a best mode, the written description must disclose the best mode in such a manner that a person of ordinary skill in the art could practice the best mode.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2165 et seq. for additional guidance. Deficiencies related to disclosure of the best mode are not usually encountered during examination because evidence to support such a deficiency is seldom in the record. (Cite: Fonar Corp. v. General Elec. Co.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty under 35 U.S.C. 102
rubrics_metrics.description: Begin by comparing the claimed subject matter to what is known in the prior art; if no differences are found between the claimed invention and the prior art, the claimed invention lacks novelty and is to be rejected under 35 U.S.C. 102.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2131-2146 for specific guidance on patentability determinations under 35 U.S.C. 102. Use applicable form paragraphs and confirm a prima facie case before imposing a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nonobviousness under 35 U.S.C. 103
rubrics_metrics.description: When differences are identified between the claimed invention and the prior art, assess whether those differences would have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill in the art; if not, the claimed invention satisfies 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP §§ 2150-2159 for specific guidance on 35 U.S.C. 103. Ensure the analysis considers the knowledge possessed by a person of ordinary skill in the art and that a prima facie case is established before rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clearly communicate findings, conclusions and their bases in Office actions
rubrics_metrics.description: Office actions should clearly communicate the findings, conclusions and reasons which support any objections or rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should use the applicable form paragraphs in Office actions to state the basis for any objections or rejections to reduce the chance of a misunderstanding as to the grounds of objection or rejection. Review proposed rejections and confirm a prima facie case of unpatentability exists before imposing a rejection.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting prohibition
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant may obtain only one patent for the same invention; identical subject matter claimed in more than one application to the same applicant is prohibited and forms the basis for statutory double patenting rejections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 804 for full discussion. Use form paragraphs 8.30, 8.31 and 8.32 for statutory double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventorship / naming of inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: The inventor(s) must be the applicant (for applications filed before Sept. 16, 2012, except as provided) and each inventor must be identified in applications filed on or after Sept. 16, 2012.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See MPEP § 2109 for details on inventorship and MPEP § 602.01(c) et seq. for correction of inventorship. In rare situations where the application does not name the correct inventorship and the applicant has not filed a correction under 37 CFR 1.48, the examiner should reject the claims under appropriate statutes (e.g., 35 U.S.C. 101 and 115 for AIA apps or pre-AIA 102(f)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Subject matter eligibility (two-criterion test under 35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Two criteria: (a) the claimed invention must fall within one of the four statutory categories (process, machine, manufacture, composition of matter); and (b) the claimed invention must be directed to patent-eligible subject matter and not to a judicial exception unless the claim as a whole includes additional limitations amounting to significantly more than the exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judicial exceptions are abstract ideas, laws of nature, and natural phenomena (including products of nature). Use the Alice/Mayo two-part test for evaluating judicial exceptions (Step 2A/2B). See MPEP § 2106 and subsections for framework and detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic Energy Act exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: No patent shall be granted for any invention or discovery which is useful solely in the utilization of special nuclear material or atomic energy in an atomic weapon (42 U.S.C. 2181(a)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applications that disclose or appear to disclose inventions relating to atomic energy are reported to the Department of Energy under 37 CFR 1.14(d). All rejections based upon sections 151(a), 152, and 155 of the Atomic Energy Act must be made only by Technology Center work group 3640 personnel.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility requirement (35 U.S.C. 101)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed invention must be useful or have a utility that is specific, substantial and credible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A rejection for lack of utility is appropriate when (1) it is not apparent why the invention is useful because applicant failed to identify any specific and substantial utility and there is no well established utility, or (2) an asserted specific and substantial utility is not credible. Such rejections can include inoperativeness (e.g., perpetual motion). Do not base a lack-of-utility rejection on grounds that the invention is frivolous, fraudulent, or against public policy. See MPEP § 2107 and subsections for guidance and form paragraphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Living subject matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Living subject matter may be patent-eligible if it is directed to a statutory category and is not excluded as a product of nature; discoveries possessing 'markedly different characteristics from any found in nature' may be eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: See Chakrabarty (genetically engineered bacterium) and subsequent cases (e.g., Myriad, Roslin). Use the 'markedly different characteristics' analysis to determine eligibility for nature-based products. See MPEP §§ 2106.03 and 2106.04(b)-(c) for detailed guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Human organisms excluded from patenting (AIA sec. 33(a))
rubrics_metrics.description: Notwithstanding any other provision of law, no patent may issue on a claim directed to or encompassing a human organism; if the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claimed invention encompasses a human organism, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101 and AIA sec. 33(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use form paragraph 7.04.03 to reject a claim under 35 U.S.C. 101 and section 33(a). Explain in the Office action why the claim is interpreted to read on a human organism and follow the examiner notes for bracketed insertions and plurality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use Alice/Mayo two-part test for judicial exceptions
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claims are directed to an abstract idea, law of nature, or natural phenomenon (Step 2A). If so, determine whether the claim recites additional elements that amount to significantly more than the judicial exception (Step 2B), i.e., search for an 'inventive concept.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Alice/Mayo two-part test is the test that should be used to evaluate eligibility. The machine-or-transformation test and other older tests may be considered only as part of the 'integration' or 'significantly more' analysis, not as separate tests. Do not rely on superseded tests like 'useful, concrete, and tangible result' or the Alappat 'special purpose computer' rationale as standalone eligibility tests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish the Broadest Reasonable Interpretation (BRI) before eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction under the broadest reasonable interpretation of the claim as a whole must be established prior to examining a claim for eligibility because BRI sets the boundaries of coverage sought and influences whether the claim covers subject matter beyond the statutory categories or encompasses judicial exceptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluating eligibility based on the BRI ensures eligibility does not depend on the draftsman's art. See MPEP § 2111. Claim interpretation examples (Mentor Graphics, Synopsys, Enfish, etc.) illustrate how BRI affects both Step 1 and the Alice/Mayo analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim interpretation's effect on eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretation of claim terms can determine whether a claim falls within a statutory category or is directed to a judicial exception, and can affect whether additional elements amount to 'significantly more.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Mentor Graphics (machine-readable medium construed to cover carrier waves -> non-statutory), Synopsys (claims interpreted as pure mental steps -> abstract idea), Enfish and McRO (constructions showing improvements in technology -> not directed to an abstract idea), Amdocs (term construction showing unconventional technical solution -> amounts to significantly more). Use specification and claim construction rules (including 35 U.S.C. 112(f) where applicable) in analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility flowchart and three eligibility pathways (A/B/C)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow a two-step eligibility analysis (Step 1: statutory category; Step 2: Alice/Mayo test) and determine eligibility via one of three pathways: A (self-evident eligibility), B (Step1 YES and Step2A NO), or C (Step1 YES, Step2A YES, and Step2B YES). If none apply, reject under 35 U.S.C. 101.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pathway A: streamlined analysis for self-evident eligibility (see MPEP § 2106.06). Pathway B: claims fall within a statutory category and are not directed to a judicial exception. Pathway C: claims fall within a statutory category, are directed to a judicial exception, but recite additional elements that amount to significantly more. If uncertain, examiners are encouraged to conduct the full eligibility analysis. Regardless of 101 outcome, complete examination under 35 U.S.C. 102, 103, 112 and utility/double patenting issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Eligibility Step 1: The four statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Confirm that the claim falls within one of the four statutory categories enumerated by 35 U.S.C. 101: processes, machines, manufactures, and compositions of matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claim covers material not found in any of the four statutory categories, it falls outside the scope of § 101 even if new and useful. See MPEP § 2106.03 for detailed information on the categories.
